items.prose: A share is quoted £29.97 bid and £30.03 ask. You buy £25,000 of it and sell it later at the same quotes.
items.question: What did the round trip cost in spreads, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the spread in bp of the mid, then apply it to £25,000.

byKey.once: You charged one side. A round trip pays the whole spread.
byKey.percent: You read the 20 bp as 20%. It is 0.2%.

explain.text: The spread is 6p on a £30.00 mid: 20 bp. A round trip pays all of it: $25{,}000 \times 0.0020 = \text{£}50$.

items.prose: Best bid £20.00 for 800 shares; best ask £20.02 for 3,200 shares.
items.question: What is the microprice? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each price by the other side's size.

byKey.mid: That is the mid. The ask holds four times the bid's size, so the microprice leans.
byKey.own: You weighted each price by its own side, which leans towards the heavy ask: backwards.

explain.text: $I = (800 - 3{,}200)/4{,}000 = -0.6$, so $P_\mu = 20.01 - 0.6 \times 0.01 = 20.004$. The thin bid is likely to be hit first.

items.prose: The mid is £50.00. The asks are 2,000 shares at £50.02, 3,000 at £50.03 and 5,000 at £50.05. You send a market buy for 6,000 shares.
items.question: What is its slippage against the mid, in bp?

widget.label: Slippage in basis points
widget.accept: 6 bp: 18,000p over the mid on 6,000 shares is 3p a share, on £50.00.

feedback.correct: 3p a share over the mid: 6 bp, £180 in all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill level by level, find the average excess over £50.00, then divide by the mid.

byKey.top: You priced every share at the best ask. Only 2,000 are there.
byKey.last: You priced every share at the last level reached. Most filled cheaper.
byKey.simple: You averaged the three level prices equally. Weight by the shares filled at each.

explain.text: 2,000 at 2p, 3,000 at 3p and 1,000 at 5p over the mid make 18,000p, or 3p a share. On £50.00 that is 6 bp, of which 4 bp is the half-spread.

items.prose: You must buy £2m of a share whose daily volatility is 1.5%. The order is 4% of its daily volume. Use the square-root model with $c = 1$.
items.question: What impact cost does it predict, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $0.015 \times \sqrt{0.04}$, then multiply by £2m.

byKey.bp: That is the impact in bp. Apply it to the £2m.

explain.text: $\sqrt{0.04} = 0.2$, so impact is $0.015 \times 0.2 = 0.003$, 30 bp. On £2m that is £6,000.

items.prose: A strategy turns over its portfolio 500% a year. Its shares have spreads of 8 bp, and it always trades with market orders.
items.question: What do spreads cost it a year, in bp of the portfolio?

widget.label: Annual spread cost in basis points
widget.accept: 40 bp: $5 \times 8$, one full spread per turnover.

feedback.correct: Five round trips at 8 bp: 40 bp a year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each turnover is a sell and a buy, which together cost one full spread.

byKey.once: You charged half a spread per turnover. A turnover has a sell and a buy: two halves.
byKey.double: You charged the full spread on each side. Each side pays half.

explain.text: Each turnover is a sell and a buy at 4 bp each: 8 bp. Five turnovers cost 40 bp, or 0.4% a year.

items.prose: You must sell £3m of one of these shares today.
items.question: Which is the better choice, and why?

options.text: L: £3m is 2.5% of its volume, against 75% of K's
K: its spread is a third of L's
options.why: You judged by spread alone. £3m is three quarters of K's whole day, so impact dwarfs the spread.

options.text: Either: the spreads and volumes trade off evenly
options.why: They do not. The order's share of volume differs thirtyfold.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the order with each share's depth and volume.

explain.text: In K the order is 75% of a day's trading and 200 times the depth at the bid. In L it is 2.5% of volume. A tight spread with no depth is expensive for a large order.

items.prose: A book has mid £10.00, a 2p spread and imbalance $I = -0.5$.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: The microprice is £9.995; the next mid move is more likely down
The microprice is £10.005; the next mid move is more likely up
options.why: You read the sign backwards. Negative imbalance means more size on the ask, so the thin bid is likely to go.

options.text: The microprice is £9.99, the best bid
options.why: You moved by $I$ times the whole spread. The shift is $I$ times half the spread.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $P_\mu = m + I\,s/2$.

explain.text: $P_\mu = 10.00 + (-0.5)(0.01) = 9.995$. It sits below the mid because the bid is thin and likely to be hit first.

items.prose: A fund holds £12m of a share that trades £20m a day. To limit impact, it sells at most 20% of daily volume.
items.question: How many trading days does the exit take?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the position by 20% of daily volume.

byKey.no-p: You used the whole day's volume. The fund sells only 20% of it.
byKey.ten: You used 10% participation. This fund allows 20%.

explain.text: 20% of £20m is £4m a day, so £12m takes 3 days. Each of those days the unsold part is exposed to the market.

items.prose: A manager decides to buy 5,000 shares when the mid is £40.00. Only 3,000 fill, at £40.06. The rest never trade, and the share closes at £39.90.
items.question: What is the implementation shortfall, in £?

widget.label: Implementation shortfall in pounds
widget.accept: −£20: £180 paid on the fills, less £200 saved on the 2,000 never bought.

feedback.correct: −£20: the missed shares happened to get cheaper.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the fills' cost over £40.00 to the move on the 2,000 missed shares.

byKey.filled-only: You costed only the fills. The 2,000 missed shares fell 10p, which the paper portfolio would have lost.
byKey.sign: You added the missed shares' move as a cost. The price fell, so missing them helped.

explain.text: Fills: $3{,}000 \times 6\text{p} = \text{£}180$. Missed: $2{,}000 \times (39.90 - 40.00) = -\text{£}200$. The shortfall is −£20; luck, not skill, since the price could as easily have risen.
